definition: In machine learning, ensemble averaging is the process of creating multiple models (typically artificial neural networks) and combining them to produce a desired output, as opposed to creating just one model.
details: Ensembles of models often outperform individual models, as the various errors of the ensemble constituents "average out".

explainer.lead: Ensemble averaging combines the outputs of several machine-learning models instead of relying on one. Their different errors can partly average out, so the combined result often performs better than an individual model.

tiers.eli5: Like asking several friends to guess how many sweets are in a jar and averaging their guesses — the group usually lands closer than any one person.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers train multiple models, often with different initialisations, and average their predictions at inference time. The pitfall is cost: every extra member adds training time, memory, and latency for a gain that may be small.
tiers.paperLevel: Given models f1...fn, the ensemble output is the average of their outputs, for example (1/n) * sum of fi(x). It improves results only when member errors are not perfectly correlated and does not guarantee improvement over the best single model.

explainer.example: Suppose three models predict numeric outputs of 0.7, 0.9, and 0.8 for the same input. Their ensemble average is (0.7 + 0.9 + 0.8) / 3 = 0.8, which becomes the combined output.

usedIn.name: Neural network prediction
usedIn.detail: Multiple neural networks can produce outputs that are combined into one prediction.

usedIn.name: Machine-learning model development
usedIn.detail: Several models can be used together when a single model's errors are undesirable.

explainer.intuition: Different models can make different mistakes on the same input. Averaging their outputs can soften those individual mistakes and produce a more useful combined result.
howItWorks: Create multiple models, typically artificial neural networks.
Give every model the same input.
Average the outputs to produce the ensemble's result.
explainer.whyItMatters: It offers a straightforward way to combine models, and ensembles often outperform individual models because constituent errors can average out.
misconceptions: It is not one model producing several outputs; it uses multiple models.
Combining models does not guarantee better performance, although ensembles often outperform individual models.
